title: Feet toward the Kaaba
hookLine: resting at Mecca, Nanak is told to move his feet away from God's house, and asks where God is not (Janamsakhi tradition)
last: BREAD THAT DRIPS MILK, NOT BLOOD.

cards: There's usually a place where you lower your voice without being told. A church, a mosque, a temple, a grandmother's living room, a grave. Something in the body knows to be careful there.
And you've probably seen someone get it wrong: shoes on where they should be off, a laugh at the wrong moment, feet up on the wrong chair.
Today's story, from the Sikh tradition, starts with exactly that kind of moment: a tired traveler at the holiest place in Islam, lying down with his feet pointing the wrong way.

teach.b: The Janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak from yesterday, say that on one of his long journeys he traveled west, as far as Mecca.
Muslim histories don't record this visit, and historians debate whether it happened as told. But Sikhs have loved the story for centuries.
Nanak arrives tired and lies down to sleep near the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine at the center of the Grand Mosque, which Muslims around the world face when they pray. His feet point toward it.
A local religious official finds him, upset, and you can see why: to him it looks like deep disrespect. He tells Nanak to take his feet away from the house of God.
And Nanak answers, as the story is told: then please turn my feet in a direction where God is not.

teach.h: HIS FEET POINT AT THE KAABA.
teach.b: In some versions, the official grabs his feet and drags them around, and wherever they point, the Kaaba seems to be there. In others, the words alone are enough. Either way, the official goes quiet.
Here's what makes the story generous rather than a put-down: Muslims teach this too. The Kaaba is the direction of prayer, the house dedicated to God, not a place God is kept.

teach.h: TURN THEM WHERE GOD IS NOT.
teach.b: The Qur'an says that to God belong the east and the west, and wherever you turn, there is the face of God.

teach.h: WHEREVER YOU TURN, THE FACE OF GOD.
teach.b: So the official and the Guru aren't really on opposite sides. Nanak just asked the question out loud, and it travels anywhere.
If there's something sacred, where is it not? The kitchen floor. The bus.
The ground under your feet right now.

how: Sikhs tell the Mecca story from the Janamsakhis to teach that God is present everywhere; Muslims face the Kaaba in prayer as the direction that unites them, while teaching that God is not confined to any place.

games.why: then turn my feet where God is not. in some tellings, wherever his feet are turned, the Kaaba seems to be there.

practice: Sit or stand with both feet flat, and notice the soles of your feet: the pressure, the temperature, the floor pushing back. Whatever this ground is, carpet, concrete, grass, it's holding you up without being asked.
If you have a sense of the sacred, ask Nanak's question quietly, is it here too, and if you don't, simply notice being held.

wordCard.voice: Kaaba. Guru Nanak's answer when told to move his feet from God's house: then turn them where God is not.
